extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, natural philosophers, and students of classical/mechanical philosophy (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the formal hypotheses, propositions, and explanatory scholia from Newton's De Mundi Systemate (Book III excerpt) covering acoustics, fluid vortices, and celestial mechanics (hypotheses and theorems about planetary motion and gravity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. L. Prob. XIII — Invenire pulsuum distantias
rubrics_metrics.description: “Invenire pulsuum distantias. Corporis, cujus tremore pulsus excitantur, inveniatur numerus Vibrationum dato tempore. Per numerum illum dividatur spatium quod pulsus eodem tempore percurrere possit, & pars inventa erit pulsus unius latitudo.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: count number of vibrations of the vibrating body in a given time; divide the distance sound travels in that time by that number to obtain the width (wavelength) of a single pulse. (Q. E. I.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of sound as propagated air-pulses
rubrics_metrics.description: “Soni vero ... nihil aliud sunt quàm aeris pulsus propagati” — sound consists of pulses propagated in the air produced by vibrating bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatory notes: Light propagates in straight lines and cannot consist in a single action; sounds originate from trembling bodies and are air pulses; stronger and lower (grave) bodies excite more noticeable tremors; faster, briefer tremors are harder to excite. Resonance: striking an object in unison with sounding bodies excites tremors (e.g., tympani, organ pipes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed of sound estimation via densities and pendulum/experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument and computations estimating the speed of sound using relative specific weights (densities) of mercury, rain water and air and pendulum-period comparisons, with references to Mersenne and Robervallus observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton computes a theoretical speed (~920–1085 English feet per second by his refined observations) and compares with experimental reports (Mersenne, Robervallus) that vary widely; notes empirical spread and finds his computed range to be consistent with phenomena. Includes concrete numerical method: relate atmospheric column heights and pendulum lengths to infer distances sound travels per second.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of partial vacuum on sound intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation: “vasa aere omni evacuari vix possunt; & ubi satis evacuantur soni notabiliter imminui solent” — when a vessel is sufficiently evacuated of air, sounds in it are markedly diminished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental test proposed: compare two equally sounding bodies, one in an evacuated vessel and one in free air, placing the listener so that distances to the two bodies are in the inverse ratio of the air densities; if the sound from the evacuated vessel does not exceed the other, the proposed scaling holds. Predicts that if only 1/100 of air remains, sound should be a hundred times weaker (equivalent to moving tenfold farther in free air).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulse spacing and organ-pipe relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical claim: pulses per unit distance and pulse width relate to organ-pipe lengths (Mersenne’s experiments). Example: Mersenne found 104 pulses in 968 feet, implying a pulse occupies about 9¼ feet; Newton concludes pulse widths in open pipes equal roughly twice the pipe lengths: “latitudines pulsuum, in omnium apertarum fistularum sonis, æquentur duplis longitudinibus fistularum.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of observed pulse counts and organ-pipe resonances to estimate pulse length; gives a plausible generalization for open pipes: pulse width ~ 2×pipe length. Also discusses pendulum-echo observations to bound speed and pulse spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis: resistance proportional to relative velocity (Sect. IX hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothesis: “Resistentiam, quæ oritur ex defectu lubricitatis partium Fluidi, cæteris paribus, proportionalem esse velocitati, qua partes Fluidi separantur ab invicem.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes internal resistance (due to lack of lubricity between fluid elements) is proportional to the velocity with which fluid parts separate; this hypothesis is used to derive subsequent theorems about motion in fluids (caveat: Newton later discusses how departures from this proportionality would alter results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LI (Theor. XXXVIII) — Rotating infinite cylinder in fluid: periods ∝ radius
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: if an infinitely long solid cylinder rotates uniformly about its axis in an infinite homogeneous fluid and each fluid part persists in its motion, then the periodic times of fluid particles are proportional to their distances from the axis of the cylinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration divides fluid into concentric cylindrical shells considered solid; using the hypothesis about resistance and mutual impressions, Newton shows angular motions are inversely proportional to distances and hence periods proportional to distances. Corollaries: angular motions of parts are reciprocally proportional to their distances, absolute velocities equal for concentric shells; adding or removing a common angular motion does not change relative motions; motion propagates gradually from inner to outer cylinders; if outer cylinder is held, inner cylinder's motion may be retarded; these phenomena are testable in deep water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LII (Theor. XXXIX) — Rotating sphere in fluid: periods ∝ (distance)^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: if a solid sphere rotates uniformly about an axis in an infinite homogeneous fluid and fluid parts persist in their motions, then the periodic times of fluid particles are proportional to the squares of their distances from the center of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof considers concentric spherical shells (or annuli) and demonstrates that translations between neighboring shells scale inversely as surface areas (∝ distance^2), giving periods ∝ distance^2. Extensive corollaries: angular motions of fluid parts reciprocally as squares of distances; propagation of rotational motion across the fluid; requirement of an active principle to sustain vortices indefinitely; behavior if a second body is introduced; consequences for enclosed spherical vessels; if the vessel and fluid are free they will undergo motion unless constrained; many corollaries discuss propagation, conservation, and eventual decay without continual impressing forces. Scholium: Newton argues these laws for vorticose media produce period–distance relations incompatible with the sesquialteral (3/2 power) Keplerian law of planetary motion unless fluid properties vary with radius or resistance increases nonlinearly — casting doubt on vortex explanations of planetary orbits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LIII (Theor. XL) — Bodies carried in a vortex return to same orbit only if same density
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: bodies transported in a vortex that return to the same orbit are of the same density as the vortex and move by the same law as its parts (with respect to velocity and orbital determination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument by imagin­ing a small vortex portion frozen (solid) and then resolved: if the solid has same density as surrounding vortex-fluid, it will move with the same law; if denser it will tend to recede from center and spiral outward, if rarer it will approach center. Corollaries: such a solid relatively rests in the surrounding fluid; if vortex is density-uniform a body may revolve at any distance. Scholium: uses this to argue planets cannot be carried by corporeal vortices because planetary motions (Keplerian) are inconsistent with vortex kinematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis I (De Mundi Systemate) — Parsimonious causes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Causas rerum naturalium non plures admitti debere, quàm quæ & vera sint & earum Phænomenis explicandis sufficiunt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle of parsimony: natural philosophy should admit no more causes than are true and sufficient to explain phenomena (heuristic methodological hypothesis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis II — Like effects have like causes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ideoque effectuum naturalium ejusdem generis eædem sunt causæ.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological principle: similar natural effects are assumed to have the same causes (applies across examples: respiration in humans and animals; descent of stones in Europe and America; light in fires and the sun; reflection on earth and planets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis III — Transformability of bodies and continuity of qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: “Corpus omne in alterius cujuscunque generis corpus transformari posse, & qualitatum gradus omnes intermedios sucessivè induere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes bodies can transform into any other kind and that gradations of qualities exist continuously; used as a general metaphysical premise for physical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis IV — Center of the world-system at rest
rubrics_metrics.description: “Centrum Systematis Mundani quiescere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted as a working hypothesis (choice of inertial frame): the center of the world-system is taken as at rest (consistent with either Earth-centered or Sun-centered representations when used appropriately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis V — Satellites of Jupiter obey area law and sesquialteral period–distance law
rubrics_metrics.description: “Planetas circumjoviales, radiis ad centrum Jovis ductis, areas describere temporibus proportionales, eorumque tempora periodica esse in ratione sesquialtera distantiarum ab ipsius centro.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of observational law for Jupiter’s satellites: areas swept by radii about Jupiter proportional to time; orbital periods follow the 3/2 power (Kepler’s third law). Newton cites observations (Flamsteed, Cassini, Borelli) to justify numerical agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis VI — Primary planets orbit the Sun (enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Planetas quinque primarios Mercurium, Venerem, Martem, Jovem & Saturnum Orbibus suis Solem cingere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declares that the five primary planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) circle the Sun, justified by observed phases and other phenomenology (e.g., Venus and Mercury phases demonstrate heliocentric motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis VII — Primary planets (and Earth/Sun models) obey Keplerian period–distance law
rubrics_metrics.description: “Planetarum quinque primariorum, & (vel Solis circa Terram vel) Terræ circa Solem tempora periodica esse in ratione sesquialtera mediocrium distantiarum à Sole.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kepler’s third law applied to the primary planets: periods are in the sesquialteral ratio of the mean distances from the Sun. Newton notes observational agreement and references Kepler and Bullialdus for orbital dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis VIII — Area law relative to Earth vs Sun
rubrics_metrics.description: “Planetas primarios radiis ad Terram ductis areas temporibus minimè proportionales; at radiis ad Solem ductis areas temporibus proportionales percurrere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational note: with respect to the Earth planets can appear to retrograde or stand still (so areas w.r.t. Earth are not simply proportional to time), but with respect to the Sun the area law (Keplerian) holds; used to justify heliocentric area-proportional motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis IX — Moon describes area proportional to time about Earth's center
rubrics_metrics.description: “Lunam radio ad centrum terræ ducto aream tempori proportionalem describere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that the Moon’s motion about the Earth obeys an area law (areas swept by radius to Earth's center proportional to time), with small perturbations from the Sun neglected for the present hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. I (Theor. I) — Forces retaining Jupiter’s satellites are directed to Jupiter and ∝ 1/r^2
rubrics_metrics.description: “Vires, quibus Planetæ circumjoviales perpetuo retrahuntur à motibus rectilineis & in orbibus suis retinentur, respicere centrum Jovis, & esse reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum locorum ab eodem centro.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton asserts that the centripetal forces keeping Jupiter’s satellites in orbit are directed to Jupiter and vary inversely as the squares of distances; proof follows from Hypothesis V and earlier propositions in Book I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II (Theor. II) — Forces retaining primary planets directed to Sun and ∝ 1/r^2
rubrics_metrics.description: “Vires, quibus Planetæ primarii perpetuo retrahuntur à motibus rectilineis, & in Orbibus suis retinentur, respicere Solem, & esse reciproce ut quadrata distantiarum ab ipsius centro.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By combining the area law (Hypoth. VIII) and Kepler’s period–distance law (Hypoth. VII), Newton demonstrates that the central forces restraining planetary motion toward the Sun are inverse-square in distance. He emphasizes the high sensitivity of apsidal motion to deviations from inverse-square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III (Theor. III) — Lunar centripetal force towards Earth ∝ 1/D^2
rubrics_metrics.description: “Vim qua Luna retinetur in Orbe suo respicere terram, & esse reciprocò ut quadratum distantiæ locorum ab ipsius centro.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton argues the force retaining the Moon in its orbit refers to the Earth and varies (to very high approximation) with the inverse square of the lunar distance. He mentions small deviations (exponent 2 - 4/243) are negligible for practical purposes; solar perturbations are handled separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IV (Theor. IV) — The Moon gravitates to the Earth (Lunam gravitare in terram)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Lunam gravitare in terram, & vi gravitatis retrahi semper à motu rectilineo, & in orbe suo retineri.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement that the Moon is attracted toward the Earth by gravitational force which continually alters its straight-line motion, keeping it in orbit. Newton discusses lunar distance estimates (various values from astronomers) and notes corrections/uncertainties in parallax and refraction affecting the numerical value but not the validity of the inverse-square gravitational conclusion.
